{{Short description|Method of studying dynamical systems}}
'''Anti-integrability''' is a method used to study the chaotic bounds of a [[dynamical system]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bolotin |first=S V |author-link=Sergey Bolotin|last2=Treschev |first2=D V |author-link2=Dmitrii Treschev|date=2015-12-31 |title=The anti-integrable limit |url=https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=rm&paperid=9692&option_lang=eng |journal=Russian Mathematical Surveys |volume=70 |issue=6 |pages=975–1030 |doi=10.1070/RM2015v070n06ABEH004972 |issn=0036-0279|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A [[dynamical system]] is at the '''anti-integrable limit''' if it becomes [[Singularity (mathematics)|singular]] and trajectories of the [[dynamical system]] no longer have an explicit form. In other words, the system becomes [[Nondeterministic algorithm|non-deterministic]] and reduces to an [[Implicit function|implicit]] relation with multiple solutions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sterling |first=D. |last2=Dullin |first2=H.R. |last3=Meiss |first3=J. D. |date=20 October 1999 |title=Homoclinic bifurcations for the Hénon map|url=https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(99)00125-6 |journal=Physica D |volume=134 |issue=2 |pages=153–184}}</ref> The significance of this limit is that, under some conditions, trajectories at the anti-integrable limit, referred to as anti-integrable states, can persist onto trajectories of the original [[dynamical system]]. Thus, anti-integrability provides a way to rigorously prove the existence of [[Chaos theory|chaotic]] orbits<ref name="l116">{{cite journal | last=Chen | first=Yi-Chiuan | title=A Proof of the Persistence of Anti-integrable States for Three-Dimensional Quadratic Diffeomorphisms | journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Dynamical Systems | volume=24 | issue=2 | date=2025-06-30 | issn=1536-0040 | doi=10.1137/24M1641695 | pages=1352–1377 | url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/24M1641695 | access-date=2026-08-05| url-access=subscription }}</ref> and to study [[Perturbation theory|perturbations]] of a [[dynamical system]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hampton |first=Amanda E. |date=2026-01-08 |title=An anti-integrable limit of a perturbed canonical McMillan map |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0297388 |journal=Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=013110 |doi=10.1063/5.0297388 |issn=1054-1500|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Statement ==

The term anti-integrability was formalized in 1990 in the field of [[Solid-state physics|solid state physics]] by Aubry and Abramovici as a method that 'opposed' [[Integrable system#Hamiltonian systems and Liouville integrability|integrability]].<ref name=aubry>{{Cite journal |last=Aubry |first=Serge |last2=Abramovici |first2=Gilles |date=1990-07-01 |title=Chaotic trajectories in the standard map. The concept of anti-integrability |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/016727899090133A |journal=Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=199–219 |doi=10.1016/0167-2789(90)90133-A |issn=0167-2789}}</ref> It was first defined in the context of [[Discrete system|discrete]] [[Lagrangian system]]s, or (locally) symplectic maps.

Trajectories of a [[Discrete system|discrete]] symplectic system, <math>\{x_t\}</math> for <math>t\in\mathbb{Z}</math>, can be found via the [[Action principles|principle of least action]]. The [[Action (physics)|action]] of a trajectory, <math>S(\{x_t\})</math>, can be written as a sum of [[Discrete system|discrete]] Lagrangians <math>L(x_t,x_{t+1})</math>, which are combinations of [[Kinetic energy|kinetic]] <math>K(x_t-x_{t+1})</math> and [[Potential energy|potential]] <math>V(x_t)</math> energies,

<math>S(\{x_t\})=\sum_tL(x_t,x_{t+1})=\sum_t \left( K(x_t-x_{t+1})-V(x_t) \right)</math>.

=== Definition for discrete Lagrangian systems ===
According to Aubry and Abramovici,<ref name=aubry /> a symplectic [[dynamical system]] with trajectories <math>\{x_t\}</math> and discrete time <math>t\in\mathbb{Z}</math> is '''anti-integrable''' when its [[Action (physics)|action]] (or generating function) <math>\sum_tL(x_{t},x_{t+1})</math> can be written as <math>\sum_tV(x_t)</math>.

The dynamics of the map governing <math>x_t\mapsto x_{t+1}</math> are considered [[Integrable system#Hamiltonian systems and Liouville integrability|integrable]] when the [[potential energy]] vanishes, and solutions can be found via the law of conservation of [[momentum]]. In contrast, the anti-integrable limit can be interpreted as the kinetic energy vanishing.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2022|volume=22|issue=1|title=Anti-integrability for Three-Dimensional Quadratic Maps |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/21M1433289 |journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Dynamical Systems |language=en |doi=10.1137/21M1433289|first=Amanda E. |last=Hampton |first2=James D. |last2=Meiss|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Following the [[Action principles|principle of least action]], trajectories of the map at the anti-integrable limit must lie at [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical points]] of the potential energy and the 'dynamics' become [[Nondeterministic algorithm|non-deterministic]], reducing to the [[shift operator]] acting on the set of these critical points. Trajectories at this limit, referred to as anti-integrable states, can then be analytically or [[Numerical continuation|numerically continued]] toward [[Integrable system#Hamiltonian systems and Liouville integrability|integrability]]. This process is similar to perturbing an integrable system via [[Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem|KAM theory]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sterling |first=D. |last2=Meiss |first2=J. D. |date=1998-04-20 |title=Computing periodic orbits using the anti-integrable limit |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0375960198000942 |journal=Physics Letters A |volume=241 |issue=1 |pages=46–52 |doi=10.1016/S0375-9601(98)00094-2 |issn=0375-9601|arxiv=chao-dyn/9802014 }}</ref>  [[Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem|KAM theory]] is used to find regular solutions that persist away from integrability, when more and more solutions become irregular. In contrast, the theory of anti-integrability is used to find irregular solutions that persist away from the anti-integrable limit, when more and more solutions become regular.

==== Example: Standard map ====

Written as a single difference equation, the [[standard map]] is given as <ref> {{Cite journal | last= Chirikov |first=Boris V. | title=A universal instability of many-dimensional oscillator systems | journal=Physics reports |url = https://doi.org/10.1016/0370-1573(79)90023-1|date= May 1979|volume = 52| issue = 5|pages= 263-379}}</ref>

<math>x_{t+1}-2x_t+x_{t-1}=\lambda\sin{x_t}</math>,

for <math>x_t\in\mathbb{R}</math> modulo <math>2\pi</math> and <math>\lambda>0</math>. The Lagrangian of this difference equation takes the form

<math>L(x_t,x_{t+1})= K(x_t-x_{t+1})-V(x_t)=(x_t-x_{t+1})^2-2\lambda\cos{x_t}.</math>

In accordance with the [[Action principles|principle of least action]], trajectories of the [[standard map]] lie at the [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical points]] of the sum of Lagrangians, i.e., where

<math>\frac{\partial}{\partial x_n}\sum_tL(x_t,x_{t+1})=0</math>

for any <math>n\in\mathbb{Z}</math>. This condition on the Lagrangian above reproduces the standard map.

The anti-integrable limit of the [[standard map]] is the limit <math>\lambda\to\infty</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Treschev |first=Dmitry |first2=Oleg|last2=Zubelevich|chapter=The Anti-Integrable Limit |date=2009 |title=Introduction to the Perturbation Theory of Hamiltonian Systems |pages=131–142 |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-642-03028-4_7 |access-date=2026-08-06 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-03028-4_7 |isbn=978-3-642-03027-7 }}</ref> To find this limit, we rescale the [[parameter]] as <math>\lambda=\frac{1}{\epsilon}</math> so that it becomes

<math>\epsilon(x_{t+1}-2x_t+x_{t-1})=\sin{x_t}.</math>

The corresponding Lagrangian is now

<math>L(x_t,x_{t+1})=\epsilon(x_t-x_{t+1})^2-2\cos{x_t}</math>.

With this rescaling, the anti-integrable limit is now the limit <math>\epsilon\to0</math>. Applying this limit and the [[Action principles|principle of least action]] leads to the [[Nondeterministic algorithm|non-deterministic]], [[Implicit function|implicit]] relation

<math>\sin{x_t}=0,</math>

with solutions <math>m\pi</math> for integer <math>m</math>. Valid anti-integrable states then come in the form

<math>\{\ldots,  m_{-1}\pi,  m_0\pi,  m_1\pi, \ldots\} \quad \text{for} \quad m_n\in\mathbb{Z},</math>

and the dynamics reduce to the [[shift operator]] on these states.

Arguments using the [[implicit function theorem]] and [[Banach fixed-point theorem|contraction mapping theorem]] can then be made to show that anti-integrable states can persist for small <math>\epsilon>0</math>, as discussed in Aubry and Abramovici's formative work.<ref name=aubry />

The definition above was generalized by Aubry in 1995<ref name=aubry95>{{Cite journal |last=Aubry |first=Serge |date=1995-09-01 |title=Anti-integrability in dynamical and variational problems |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/016727899500109H |journal=Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena |volume=86 |issue=1 |pages=284–296 |doi=10.1016/0167-2789(95)00109-H |issn=0167-2789|url-access=subscription }}</ref> to include all [[Discrete system|discrete]] maps. This generalized definition provides an alternative, and arguably easier, approach to implement anti-integrability, as can be seen in the example of the [[logistic map]]  below.

=== Definition for general discrete maps ===
Consider a one [[parameter]] <math>\epsilon</math>-[[Continuous function|continuous]] family of deterministic [[dynamical system]]s <math>X_{t+1}=F_\epsilon(X_t)</math>. The limit <math>\epsilon\to0</math> is called the '''anti-integrable limit''' when
* The system can be defined as an implicit [[dynamical system]], i.e., there exists a function <math>G_\epsilon(X,Y)</math> which depends continuously on <math>\epsilon</math> such that the [[Implicit function|implicit equation]] <math>G_\epsilon(X,Y)=0</math> is equivalent to <math>Y=F_\epsilon(X)</math> for <math>\epsilon\neq0</math> and such that the limit <math>G_0(X,Y)</math> is defined.
* The solutions <math>\{X_t\}</math> of the [[Implicit function|implicit equations]] <math>G_0(X_{t+1},X_t)=0</math> for all <math>t</math> form a [[Discrete system|discrete]] set which can be characterized by an infinite [[sequence]] <math>\{s_t\}\in\Sigma^\mathbb{Z}</math> called a coding (or [[Symbolic dynamics|symbolic]]) sequence <math>\{s_t\}\to\{X_t\}</math> where <math>s_t</math> belongs to a [[Discrete system|discrete]] set <math>\Sigma</math> of codes (or symbols).<ref name=aubry95 />

==== Example: Logistic map ====
Following the work of Chen,<ref name=chen>{{Cite journal |last=Chen |first=Yi-Chiuan |date=2007-04-01 |title=Anti-integrability for the Logistic Maps |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225445459_Anti-integrability_for_the_Logistic_Maps |journal=Chinese Annals of Mathematics, Series B |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=219–224 |doi=10.1007/s11401-005-0413-4 |issn=1860-6261}}</ref> the [[logistic map]],

<math>x_{t+1}= \mu x_t(1-x_t), \quad x\in\mathbb{R}, \quad\mu>0,</math>

has an anti-integrable limit <math>\mu\to\infty</math>. To see this, rewrite the map using the rescaling <math>\mu=\frac{1}{\epsilon}</math> to obtain

<math>x_t(1-x_t)=\epsilon x_{t+1}.</math>

The [[Singularity (mathematics)|singular]] anti-integrable limit <math>\mu\to\infty</math> now corresponds with <math>\epsilon\to 0</math>.

When <math>\epsilon=0</math>, the map becomes the [[Nondeterministic algorithm|non-deterministic]], [[Implicit function|implicit]] relation <math>x_t(1-x_t)=0</math> and has the solutions <math>x_t=0</math> or <math>x_t=1</math> for every <math>t\in\mathbb{Z}</math>. Each valid anti-integrable state is associated with a [[Symbolic dynamics|symbolic]] sequence, <math>s=\{\ldots, s_{-1},s_0,s_1,\ldots\}</math>, where <math>s_t\in\{0,1\},</math> for integer <math>t</math>. Thus, at the anti-integrable limit, the 'dynamics' become a [[Shift operator|shift]] on these two symbols.

The anti-integrable states at <math>\epsilon=0</math> persist for small <math>\epsilon>0</math>, which Chen proves analytically with an [[implicit function theorem]] argument.<ref name=chen/>

==Extensions==
Arguments for persistence away from the anti-integrable limit typically utilize the [[implicit function theorem]] or the [[Banach fixed-point theorem|contraction mapping theorem]]. One can also continue anti-integrable states away from the anti-integrable limit using [[numerical continuation]].<ref name="r730">{{cite book | last1=Krauskopf | first1=Bernd | last2=Osinga | first2=Hinke M. |author-link2=Hinke Osinga| last3=Galan-Vioque | first3=Jorge | title=Numerical Continuation Methods for Dynamical Systems: Path following and boundary value problems | publisher=Springer Netherlands Springer e-books | publication-place=Dordrecht | date=2007 | isbn=978-1-4020-6356-5 | page=17-24}}</ref>

Anti-integrability has also been used to prove the existence of a [[Horseshoe map|horseshoe]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chen |first=Yi-Chiuan |date=2006-04-01 |title=Smale horseshoe via the anti-integrability |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S096007790500545X |journal=Chaos, Solitons & Fractals |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=377–385 |doi=10.1016/j.chaos.2005.05.050 |issn=0960-0779|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and to study the development of [[Chaos theory|chaotic]] [[attractor]]s over changing [[parameter]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Connecting Anti-integrability to Attractors for Three-Dimensional Quadratic Diffeomorphisms |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/23M1571897 |journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Dynamical Systems |language=en |doi=10.1137/23M1571897|first=Amanda E. |last=Hampton |first2=James D. |last2=Meiss |volume=23|issue=1|date=2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
